content: An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is defined as a localized enlargement of the abdominal aorta, where the diameter exceeds the normal size by more than 50%. The normal diameter of the aorta varies depending on factors such as the patient’s age, sex, height, weight, race, body surface area, and baseline blood pressure. This condition is often associated with age-related degenerative changes in the vessel walls. Causes of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Life-Threatening Causes: Abdominal aortic aneurysm is a critical condition that requires immediate medical attention, regardless of the underlying cause. Potential life-threatening causes include: Abdominal trauma Bacteremia (presence of bacteria in the bloodstream) Gastrointestinal perforation Vertebral osteomyelitis (infection of the vertebrae) Common Causes: Abdominal trauma Atherosclerosis (buildup of plaque in the arteries) Marfan syndrome (a genetic disorder affecting connective tissue) Focused Initial Rapid Evaluation (FIRE) A Focused Initial Rapid Evaluation (FIRE) should be conducted to promptly identify patients who require urgent intervention. This step is critical in the management of abdominal aortic aneurysms. Complete Diagnostic Approach After the initial rapid evaluation and the initiation of any necessary urgent interventions, a comprehensive diagnostic approach should be undertaken to fully assess the condition and guide further management. Treatment The treatment of abdominal aortic aneurysms follows established clinical guidelines. These guidelines are summarized in various algorithms and studies, such as those by Solberg et al. (2001), Bufé (2013), and others. Treatment options may include endovascular repair or open surgical repair, depending on the size, location, and severity of the aneurysm, as well as the patient’s overall health status. References The information provided is supported by numerous studies and publications, including: Solberg, S. (2001). Prevalence of and risk factors for abdominal aortic aneurysms in a population-based study: The Tromsø Study. Bufé, A. (2013). Thoracal, abdominal and thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm. Greenhalgh RM, Powell JT. Endovascular repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm. N Engl J Med. Haas, MA. (2000). The accuracy of physical examination to detect abdominal aortic aneurysm. Yao, JS. (1990). Distal embolization as a presenting symptom of aortic aneurysms. Rosso, R. (2011). The challenge of posttraumatic thrombus embolization from abdominal aortic aneurysm causing acute limb ischemia. These references highlight the importance of early detection, accurate diagnosis, and timely intervention in the management of abdominal aortic aneurysms.
